visuals.heading: Five Event Segments

items.text: Job postings and course brochures often talk about "event management" as one field.
Pick a segment deliberately once you have tried more than one.

They are ordered here by real growth headroom, not by which one sounds most familiar: weddings lead because the percentage-of-budget billing model shown further down lets an established planner's income grow with the size of the event rather than the hours worked, on top of having the largest client volume of any segment; corporate events and exhibitions come next because recurring accounts and process-driven delivery are easier to systemise and hand to a team; concerts and sports sit last here because both demand specialist entry experience first, and sports events also run at lower volume in most Indian cities.
The biggest volume segment in India by number of events, and the one most people picture first.

blocks.heading: Both Entry Routes Below Are Legitimate

items.text: A useful middle path is doing both, in either order: a shorter education program alongside or right before an internship, so the classroom concepts land while you are actually applying them on real events.

blocks.heading: Not Worked an Event

items.text: If you have not worked an event yet, the honest gap is not knowledge, it is proof.
They do expect you to show you have actually stood inside an event and made real decisions, even a small one.
College fests, cultural society events, NGO fundraisers, and local business launches all need extra hands and rarely pay, but they let you stand inside a real event timeline and see what breaks.

blocks.sourceSectionTitle: Building proof with no company behind you

items.text: Pick a segment deliberately after trying more than one, instead of drifting into whichever internship you found first.
Build one piece of real event proof before you apply anywhere, it matters more than the certificate alone.

blocks.heading: Vendor Coordination: Sourcing, Negotiating With, and Managing

items.text: Budgeting: building a realistic cost sheet upfront, tracking spend against it, and knowing where to cut without the client noticing when something runs over.
Logistics: timelines, load-in and load-out schedules, permits, transport, and the dozens of small sequencing decisions that decide whether an event runs on time.
Client management: translating a vague brief into a workable plan, managing expectations honestly, and staying calm when a client changes their mind two days before the event.

On-ground execution under pressure: the actual event day, where something will go wrong, a vendor is late, the weather shifts, a VIP guest changes plans, and someone has to make a fast decision without panicking.
